title: fix(codegen): substitute vecN<T> members of specialized generic structs
issue_title: A generic struct member of type `vecN<T>` is written `T2` after specialisation
gold_patch:
diff --git a/CHANGELOG.md b/CHANGELOG.md
index 7ae05402c1..2e5d8c8081 100644
--- a/CHANGELOG.md
+++ b/CHANGELOG.md
@@ -27,6 +27,7 @@ Notable changes to CrossTL for people who install and use it, newest first. Inte
 - Slang output reads and writes a matrix in a storage buffer column by column. A loaded `mat3` was the transpose of the stored matrix, a non-square matrix such as `mat2x3` did not compile, and a store wrote rows into the buffer's columns; loads now build `transpose(float2x3(column0, column1))` and stores select each column, as the HLSL output does.
 - Slang output declares a function prototype without a body, which slangc had rejected as a second definition, and reads a structured buffer's element count with `GetDimensions(count, stride)`, the only overload slangc provides. SPIR-V output inlines the definition of a helper that takes a storage buffer instead of also counting its prototype as an overload.
 - HLSL and Slang output of `buffer_dimensions(b, count)` on a structured buffer assign the element count (`count = cgl_buffer_count(b);`) instead of calling `b.GetDimensions(count)`, which has no overload for a structured buffer and was rejected by DXC and slangc; output lists no `GetDimensions` overload takes, such as a stride for a byte-address buffer, are refused with a diagnostic.
+- HIP, Metal, HLSL and GLSL output write a generic struct member of type `vecN<T>`, such as `vec2<T> v;` in `struct VBox<T>`, with its concrete vector once the struct is specialized: `float2 v;` in HIP, Metal and HLSL output and `vec2 v;` in GLSL output, including an array of generic vectors such as `vec2<T> q[2];`. They used to write `T2 v;`, which the HIP, Metal and HLSL compilers reject with `unknown type name 'T2'` and which GLSL output refused outright (#4198).
 
 ---

+"""Generic struct members of type ``vecN<T>`` keep their concrete vector after specialisation.
+
+``struct VBox<T> { vec2<T> v; T s; }`` specialized for ``float`` declared ``T2 v;``: the generators spell the member
+``T2`` before substituting it, so Metal, HLSL, HIP and CUDA named an undeclared type and GLSL refused the program
+(issue #4198). The same spelling broke an array of generic vectors, ``vec2<T> q[2]``. Each case below fails on that
+code.
+"""
+
+import shutil
+import subprocess
+import textwrap
+
+import pytest
+
+import crosstl
+
+PROGRAM = textwrap.dedent("""
+    shader main {
+        struct VBox<T> { vec2<T> v; T s; };
+        struct IVec<T> { vec3<T> p; vec2<T> q[2]; T s; };
+        buffer float* results;
+        buffer int* iresults;
+        compute {
+        @ numthreads(1, 1, 1)
+        void main() {
+            VBox<float> b;
+            b.v = vec2(1.0, 2.0);
+            b.s = 3.0;
+            results[0] = b.v.x + b.v.y + b.s;
+            IVec<int> u;
+            u.p = vec3(1, 2, 3);
+            u.q[0] = vec2(4, 5);
+        u.q[1] = vec2(6, 7);
+            u.s = 6;
+            iresults[0] = u.p.x + u.p.y + u.p.z + u.q[0].x + u.q[1].y + u.s;
+        }
+        }
+    }
+""").strip()
+
+
+def translate(tmp_path, backend):
+    path = tmp_path / "vectors.cgl"
+    path.write_text(PROGRAM)
+    return crosstl.translate(str(path), backend=backend, format_output=False)
+
+
+def _validate(tmp_path, backend, output):
+    if backend == "opengl":
+        tool = shutil.which("glslangValidator")
+        if tool is None:
+            pytest.skip("glslangValidator is not installed")
+        path = tmp_path / "out.comp"
+        path.write_text(output)
+        command = [tool, "-S", "comp", str(path)]
+    elif backend == "metal":
+        xcrun = shutil.which("xcrun")
+        if xcrun is None:
+            pytest.skip("xcrun is not installed")
+        path = tmp_path / "out.metal"
+        path.write_text(output)
+        command = [xcrun, "-sdk", "macosx", "metal", "-c", str(path), "-o", "/dev/null"]
+    else:
+        tool = shutil.which("dxc")
+        if tool is None:
+            pytest.skip("dxc is not installed")
+        path = tmp_path / "out.hlsl"
+        path.write_text(output)
+        command = [tool, "-HV", "2021", "-T", "cs_6_2", "-E", "CSMain", str(path)]
+    result = subprocess.run(command, check=False, capture_output=True, text=True)
+    assert result.returncode == 0, result.stdout + result.stderr
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize(
+    ("backend", "declarations"),
+    [
+        (
+            "metal",
+            (
+                "struct VBox_float {\n    float2 v;\n    float s;\n};",
+                "struct IVec_int {\n    int3 p;\n    int2 q[2];\n    int s;\n};",
+            ),
+        ),
+        (
+            "directx",
+            (
+                "struct VBox_float {\n    float2 v;\n    float s;\n};",
+                "struct IVec_int {\n    int3 p;\n    int2 q[2];\n    int s;\n};",
+            ),
+        ),
+        (
+            "opengl",
+            (
+                "struct VBox_float {\n    vec2 v;\n    float s;\n};",
+                "struct IVec_int {\n    ivec3 p;\n    ivec2 q[2];\n    int s;\n};",
+            ),
+        ),
+        (
+            "hip",
+            (
+                "struct VBox_float {\n    float2 v;\n    float s;\n};",
+                "struct IVec_int {\n    int3 p;\n    int2 q[2];\n    int s;\n};",
+            ),
+        ),
+    ],
+)
+def test_specialized_vector_struct_members_are_concrete(
+    tmp_path, backend, declarations
+):
+    output = translate(tmp_path, backend)
+
+    for declaration in declarations:
+        assert declaration in output, declaration
+    assert "T2" not in output
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("backend", ["metal", "directx", "opengl"])
+def test_specialized_vector_struct_members_translate_to_valid_targets(
+    tmp_path, backend
+):
+    _validate(tmp_path, backend, translate(tmp_path, backend))

problem_statement.title: [BUG] MJCF geom solref and joint solreflimit with one value get damping ratio 0 instead of MuJoCo's 1
problem_statement.body:
### Bug Description

MuJoCo fills missing trailing `solref` components from its default (0.02, 1), so `solreflimit="0.005"` means (0.005, 1). `mujoco.MjSpec.to_xml()` writes this one-value form for any solref whose damping ratio is 1.

When `SolverMuJoCo`'s custom attributes are registered, Newton reads two of these attributes with a damping ratio of 0:

- geom `solref` -> `model.mujoco.solref`, passed on as `geom_solref`;
- joint `solreflimit` -> `model.mujoco.solreflimit`, passed on as `jnt_solref`.

A damping ratio of 0 is not a valid solref. MuJoCo C replaces such a value with its default (0.02, 1) and prints `mixed solref format, replacing with default`, so the authored time constant is lost. MuJoCo Warp has no such check: for a sphere 1 mm into a plane and a hinge 0.01 rad past its limit, `efc_aref` is 9.5e11 and 9.429e14, against 65.79 and 4.179e4 with a damping ratio of 1 (last lines of the output below). Newton warns for `solreflimit` ("Authored mujoco.solreflimit has invalid components ...") but not for geom `solref`.

So an MJCF saved by `MjSpec.to_xml()` imports with these values wherever a geom or joint-limit damping ratio was 1.

**Cause.** These attributes are parsed by the generic custom-attribute path, which pads a short vector from the attribute's registered default:

- [`solver_mujoco.py#L1685-L1698`](https://github.com/newton-physics/newton/blob/0679304388f3edfea6e7e942232724425d089cd3/newton/_src/solvers/mujoco/solver_mujoco.py#L1685-L1698) (`mujoco:solref`, shape) and [`solver_mujoco.py#L1742-L1755`](https://github.com/newton-physics/newton/blob/0679304388f3edfea6e7e942232724425d089cd3/newton/_src/solvers/mujoco/solver_mujoco.py#L1742-L1755) (`mujoco:solreflimit`, joint DOF) register `wp.vec2(0.0, 0.0)` as their "not authored" sentinel.
- [`import_utils.py#L151-L154`](https://github.com/newton-physics/newton/blob/0679304388f3edfea6e7e942232724425d089cd3/newton/_src/utils/import_utils.py#L151-L154) calls `string_to_warp(x, dtype, default)`, and [`import_utils.py#L102-L112`](https://github.com/newton-physics/newton/blob/0679304388f3edfea6e7e942232724425d089cd3/newton/_src/utils/import_utils.py#L102-L112) pads the missing component from that default, which gives 0.

The other solref-type custom attributes (`solreffriction`, `pair_solref`, `pair_solreffriction`, `tendon_solref_limit`, `tendon_solref_friction`) register (0.02, 1) and are padded correctly. The importer's own `parse_vec` already applies MuJoCo's rule ([`import_mjcf.py#L1058-L1075`](https://github.com/newton-physics/newton/blob/0679304388f3edfea6e7e942232724425d089cd3/newton/_src/utils/import_mjcf.py#L1058-L1075), `_SOLREF_SHORTHAND_KEYS`).

Related: #5030 makes partial values inherit their missing components from an authored `<default>` class. It does not cover this case, where no class sets the attribute and MuJoCo's built-in default applies. With #5030 merged onto `main`, the script below gives the same values.

**Expected.** A one-value `solref` / `solreflimit` gets the damping ratio 1, as in MuJoCo: (0.003, 1) and (0.005, 1).

### Reproduction Script

```python
"""MJCF solref / solreflimit with one value: Newton stores dampratio 0 where MuJoCo uses 1.

MuJoCo fills a missing trailing solref component from its default (0.02, 1), so solref="0.003" means (0.003, 1).
This prints the value Newton stores, the value SolverMuJoCo passes to MuJoCo, and the value MuJoCo compiles from the
same XML. Runs on CPU.
"""

import mujoco
import newton
import numpy as np
import warp as wp
from newton.solvers import SolverMuJoCo

XML = """
<mujoco>
  <worldbody>
    <body pos="0 0 1">
      <joint name="j" type="hinge" limited="true" range="-1 1" solreflimit="0.005" solreffriction="0.004"/>
      <geom name="g" type="sphere" size="0.1" mass="1" solref="0.003"/>
    </body>
  </worldbody>
</mujoco>
"""


def main() -> int:
    wp.config.quiet = True
    builder = newton.ModelBuilder()
    SolverMuJoCo.register_custom_attributes(builder)
    builder.add_mjcf(XML)
    model = builder.finalize(device="cpu")
    solver = SolverMuJoCo(model, use_mujoco_cpu=True)
    native = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(XML)
    mj = solver.mj_model

    rows = [
        ('joint solreflimit="0.005"', model.mujoco.solreflimit.numpy()[0], mj.jnt_solref[0], native.jnt_solref[0]),
        ('geom solref="0.003"', model.mujoco.solref.numpy()[0], mj.geom_solref[0], native.geom_solref[0]),
        (
            'joint solreffriction="0.004"',
            model.mujoco.solreffriction.numpy()[0],
            mj.dof_solref[0],
            native.dof_solref[0],
        ),
    ]
    print(f"newton {newton.__version__}, mujoco {mujoco.__version__}, warp {wp.__version__}")
    print(f"{'MJCF':30s} {'model.mujoco':>16s} {'SolverMuJoCo':>16s} {'MuJoCo':>16s}")
    mismatches = 0
    for name, stored, passed, ref in rows:
        bad = not np.allclose(passed, ref)
        mismatches += bad
        print(
            f"{name:30s} {np.array2string(np.asarray(stored), precision=4):>16s} "
            f"{np.array2string(np.asarray(passed), precision=4):>16s} {np.array2string(ref, precision=4):>16s}"
            f"{'  <- differs' if bad else ''}"
        )
    print(f"{mismatches} of {len(rows)} differ from MuJoCo")

    # MuJoCo's own writer emits this form: a two-value solref with dampratio 1 is saved as one value.
    spec = mujoco.MjSpec.from_string(XML.replace('"0.005"', '"0.005 1"').replace('"0.003"', '"0.003 1"'))
    written = [line.strip() for line in spec.to_xml().splitlines() if "solref" in line]
    print("MjSpec.to_xml() of the same model with explicit dampratio 1:")
    for line in written:
        print(f"  {line}")
    consequence()
    return 0


def consequence() -> None:
    """Reference accelerations (efc_aref) of a sphere 1 mm into a plane and a hinge 0.01 rad past its limit."""
    import mujoco_warp as mjw

    def build(geom_solref: str, limit_solref: str) -> mujoco.MjModel:
        return mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(f"""
<mujoco><worldbody>
  <geom type="plane" size="1 1 0.1" solref="{geom_solref}"/>
  <body pos="0 0 0.099"><freejoint/><geom type="sphere" size="0.1" mass="1" solref="{geom_solref}"/></body>
  <body pos="1 0 1"><joint type="hinge" limited="true" range="-1 1" solreflimit="{limit_solref}"/>
    <geom type="box" size="0.05 0.05 0.05" mass="1" contype="0" conaffinity="0"/></body>
</worldbody></mujoco>""")

    print("efc_aref [first contact row, joint limit], MuJoCo C vs MuJoCo Warp:")
    for geom_solref, limit_solref in (("0.003 1", "0.005 1"), ("0.003 0", "0.005 0")):
```

problem_statement.title: AsciiDoc: links in block titles stay as raw `url[text]` markup
problem_statement.body:
### Bug

Since #5115, a link like `https://example.com[Docs]` in an AsciiDoc paragraph becomes link text with a hyperlink. The same link in a block title (`.Title ...`) is not parsed. The title is added as text with the raw `https://example.com[Docs]` markup and no hyperlink.

### Steps to reproduce

```python
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from docling.document_converter import DocumentConverter

SRC = """See https://example.com[Docs]

.Caption https://example.com[Docs]
Para after title.
"""

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    p = Path(d) / "t.adoc"
    p.write_text(SRC)
    doc = DocumentConverter().convert(p).document

for t in doc.texts:
    print((t.text, str(t.hyperlink) if t.hyperlink else None))
```

Output on `main` (07154cd):

```
('See', None)
('Docs', 'https://example.com/')
('Caption https://example.com[Docs]', None)
('Para after title.', None)
```

The paragraph link becomes `Docs` with the hyperlink `https://example.com/`. The block title keeps `https://example.com[Docs]` as literal text.

Expected: the title doesn't keep the raw `url[text]` markup. I'd expect `Caption Docs`, with the link kept the way paragraphs keep it. A title is a single text item, so if a link inside it can't be represented, plain `Docs` would still be better than the raw markup. I didn't find docs saying titles keep the markup; if that's intended, feel free to close this.

### Docling version

`main` @ 07154cd (docling-slim 2.145.0). The 2.145.0 release predates #5115, so links in paragraphs are not parsed there either.

### Python version

Python 3.12.16, Linux (aarch64)

### Additional context

In `docling/backend/asciidoc_backend.py`, block title text is built with `" ".join(caption_data)` and passed straight to `doc.add_text`, without the inline parsing that `_flush_text_data` now does for paragraphs. My script reaches this in `_flush_caption_as_paragraph` (line 212). The same pattern is at line 348 (title before a list), line 656 (picture caption) and line 1122 (table caption). I read those three but did not run them.

I can send a PR that runs title and caption text through the same inline parsing, with tests for a title before a paragraph, an `image::` and a `|===` table.

problem_statement.title: Anthropic adapter: Claude Code's adaptive thinking runs uncapped on local reasoning models
problem_statement.body:
## Problem

Claude Code (headless `claude -p`, current release) sends `thinking: {"type": "adaptive", "display": "omitted"}` on every `/v1/messages` request. `_resolve_reasoning_max_tokens` in `rapid_mlx/api/anthropic_adapter.py` treats `adaptive` as "no cap", so a local reasoning model thinks without bound. `MAX_THINKING_TOKENS` on the client side has no effect because Claude Code does not send `budget_tokens` in adaptive mode.

Observed with qwen3.6-27b-4bit driving Claude Code on a coding task: single turns of 4k–12k completion tokens, thinking blocks clipped at 32,768 chars, 20–40 tool calls in 40 minutes with zero edits. That's a usable-vs-unusable difference for `rapid-mlx launch claude` on 27B-class models at ~30 tok/s.

## Evidence

- Direct request with `thinking: {type: enabled, budget_tokens: 300}` → thinking capped at ~1,200 chars (cap works).
- The same request from Claude Code arrives as `adaptive` (logged by a pass-through proxy) → uncapped.
- Rewriting `adaptive` to `enabled/1500` in a local proxy brings per-turn thinking back to ~1.5k tokens.

## Proposal

Map `adaptive` to a bounded default instead of `None`: reuse `--default-reasoning-effort` when set, otherwise a moderate per-request cap (e.g. the `medium` entry of `ANTHROPIC_EFFORT_TO_REASONING_MAX_TOKENS`). Upstream Anthropic semantics for adaptive are "model decides"; for local models at 20–40 tok/s, "model decides" means minutes per turn. Add a unit test for the adaptive branch and an e2e through `rapid-mlx launch claude`.

problem_statement.title: MemoryLockManager and FileSystemLockManager raise on release_lock after a lock expires; RedisLockManager does not
problem_statement.body:
## Description

`release_lock` on a lock whose hold timeout has elapsed raises `ValueError`, while `RedisLockManager.release_lock` deliberately treats a vanished lock as already released (its docstring: _"If the lock doesn't exist in Redis at all, this method will succeed even if the holder ID doesn't match"_ — to handle locks released during a task retry).

## Reproduction

```python
import time
from prefect.locking.memory import MemoryLockManager

manager = MemoryLockManager()
manager.acquire_lock("k", holder="h1", hold_timeout=0.1)
time.sleep(0.2)  # hold timeout elapses; the entry is dropped
manager.release_lock("k", holder="h1")
# ValueError: No lock held by h1 for transaction with key k
```

`FileSystemLockManager` behaves the same way (`No lock for transaction with key ...`).

## Impact

`Transaction.commit`/`rollback` call `store.release_lock` unguarded (`src/prefect/transactions.py`, including in a `finally:` block), so a SERIALIZABLE transaction whose lock expires mid-flight fails its own teardown — and in the `finally` path the `ValueError` masks the original exception.

Since `LockManager` implementations are interchangeable behind the same protocol, the memory and filesystem managers should match the redis semantics: releasing a lock that no longer exists is a no-op; a live lock held by a different holder still raises.

+"""Regression tests for #8862: /api/session/new must refuse a malformed profile.
+
+The route accepted ``body["profile"]`` unvalidated and forwarded it to
+``_resolve_new_session_workspace`` and ``new_session``.  A forged request could
+therefore create a session whose profile is not a profile name at all
+(non-string JSON, path-like strings, names with spaces/case).  These tests pin
+the 400 refusal and prove nothing was cached.
+"""

+from __future__ import annotations
+
+from urllib.parse import urlparse
+
+import pytest
+
+import api.models as models
+import api.routes as routes
+
+
+def _post_session_new(body: dict, monkeypatch):
+    """Drive POST /api/session/new with stubbed transport and a new_session spy."""
+    cap = {"created": []}
+
+    def _j(_handler, payload, *_, **__):
+        cap["ok"] = payload
+        return True
+
+    def _bad(_handler, msg, code=400):
+        cap["bad"] = (msg, code)
+        return True
+
+    class _Session:
+        def __init__(self, profile):
+            self.session_id = "new8862"
+            self.profile = profile
+            self.messages = []
+
+        def compact(self):
+            return {"session_id": self.session_id, "profile": self.profile}
+
+    def _new_session(**kwargs):
+        cap["created"].append(kwargs)
+        return _Session(kwargs.get("profile"))
+
+    handler = type("_Handler", (), {})()
+    handler.command = "POST"
+    handler.headers = {}
+
+    monkeypatch.setattr(routes, "read_body", lambda _h: body)
+    monkeypatch.setattr(routes, "_check_csrf", lambda _h: True)
+    monkeypatch.setattr(routes, "_csrf_exempt_path", lambda _p: False)
+    monkeypatch.setattr(routes, "_guard_request_session_visibility", lambda *_a, **_k: True)
+    monkeypatch.setattr(routes, "new_session", _new_session)
+    monkeypatch.setattr(routes, "j", _j)
+    monkeypatch.setattr(routes, "bad", _bad)
+
+    cached_before = frozenset(models.SESSIONS)
+    routes.handle_post(handler, urlparse("/api/session/new"))
+    cap["cached_after"] = frozenset(models.SESSIONS)
+    cap["cached_before"] = cached_before
+    return cap
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize(
+    "profile",
+    [
+        123,
+        True,
+        ["default"],
+        {"name": "default"},
+        "../evil",
+        "No Such Profile",
+    ],
+    ids=[
+        "int",
+        "bool",
+        "list",
+        "dict",
+        "path-like",
+        "spaces-and-case",
+    ],
+)

+    cap = _post_session_new({"profile": profile}, monkeypatch)

+    assert "ok" not in cap
+    # Nothing may be created or cached: the refusal happens before both paths
+    # that receive ``profile`` and before any worktree/session write.
+    assert cap["created"] == []
+    assert cap["cached_after"] == cap["cached_before"]
+
+
+def test_session_new_still_accepts_a_well_formed_profile(monkeypatch):
+    cap = _post_session_new({"profile": "default"}, monkeypatch)

+
+

+

+    assert "ok" in cap
+    assert [kw.get("profile") for kw in cap["created"]] == ["ghost"]

problem_statement.title: POST /api/session/new accepts a profile that isn't a valid profile name
problem_statement.body:
`POST /api/session/new` accepts a profile that isn't a valid profile name.

**Seen on:** master `f65960b46351` (exp-v0.52.641).

## What happens

`POST /api/session/new` passes `body.get("profile") or None` through unchecked (`api/routes.py` ~19394/19418/19424/19518 → `new_session(profile=...)`). The real client always sends a valid name, so this needs a crafted request. Results recorded on master, with the agent stubbed:

| `profile` sent | `/api/session/new` | cached session's `profile` | then `/api/chat/start` naming `default` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `123`, `true`, `["default"]`, `{"name": "default"}` | 200 | the raw value (int, bool, list, dict) | 200, a turn starts, and the profile stays the non-string value |
| `"../evil"`, `"No Such Profile"`, `"ghost"` | 200 | the raw string | 200, a turn starts, and the session is retagged to `default` |

- **Path traversal is already blocked downstream.** `get_hermes_home_for_profile` falls back to the default home for a name that doesn't match the profile-name format, so `"../evil"` reads no other directory. No file named after it was created in the run.
- **The real cost:** a session can exist, at least in memory, with an owner that no ownership check can read.
- **After #8853:** chat/start answers 404 for the non-string cases, because ownership is unverifiable. So the session `/api/session/new` just returned can't be used, and the request that created it got 200.

## Fix shape

Validate `profile` the way the other routes already do (chat/start, import and archive answer `400 "invalid profile"` via `_PROFILE_ID_RE`):
- **`None` or `""`:** unchanged; the active profile applies.
- **A non-string, or a string that fails `_PROFILE_ID_RE.fullmatch`:** `400 "invalid profile"` before anything is created.
- **Optional:** an unknown but well-formed name (`"ghost"`) could get the same 400, if creating a session under a profile that doesn't exist is never wanted. That's a product call; today the session is retagged on its first chat/start.

Add a test that posts each of the values above and asserts 400 with nothing cached.

Found by the senior review of #8853 (gate on `4116564cc867`), and reproduced here.

title: fix(semantics): lower an empty brace initializer of an enumeration to zero
issue_title: An empty brace initializer of an enumeration, `Mode m = {};`, is copied, written as `array()` or refused
gold_patch:
diff --git a/CHANGELOG.md b/CHANGELOG.md
index 0e3d4c7972..af2bfa9195 100644
--- a/CHANGELOG.md
+++ b/CHANGELOG.md
@@ -18,6 +18,7 @@ Notable changes to CrossTL for people who install and use it, newest first. Inte
 - WGSL output writes a structure's brace initializer, such as `Pair p = {x, 2.0};`, as the structure's value constructor, `var p: Pair = Pair(x, 2.0);`, in a declaration, an assignment, a return value, a call argument, a shader-scope constant or variable, a nested member and an array of structures. Each value is converted to its member's type, as in `Q(u32(1), i32(x))`, and the members left out are set to zero as GLSL output does. An initializer with more values than members, or one for a structure that holds an atomic or a resource, is refused with `WGSLStructInitializerError` (`project.translate.wgsl-struct-initializer-unsupported`). It used to write `array(x, 2.0)`, which naga rejects because the declared type is `Pair` (#3653).
 - WGSL output writes a vector's or a matrix's brace initializer as the type's value constructor: `vec3 v = {x, 1.0, 2.0};` becomes `var v: vec3<f32> = vec3<f32>(x, 1.0, 2.0);`, and `mat2 m = {vec2(1.0, 0.0), vec2(0.0, x)};` or `{{1.0, 0.0}, {0.0, x}}` becomes `mat2x2<f32>(vec2<f32>(1.0, 0.0), vec2<f32>(0.0, x))`, in the same places as a structure's, including a structure member, as in `V(vec3<f32>(x, 1.0, 2.0), 3.0)`, and an array of vectors. A matrix takes one vector per column or one scalar per component. Each value is converted to the component or column type, as in `vec3<f32>(f32(k), 1.0, 2.0)`, and the components a vector list leaves out are set to zero as GLSL output does. A list with more values than the vector has components, a non-scalar vector component, and a matrix list that is neither one vector per column nor one scalar per component are refused with `WGSLVectorInitializerError` (`project.translate.wgsl-vector-initializer-unsupported`). It used to write `array(x, 1.0, 2.0)`, which naga rejects because the declared type is `vec3<f32>` (#3684).
 - An empty brace initializer of a scalar variable or constant, such as `float one = {};`, `int n = {};`, `short s = {};` or `real_t one = {};` for `typedef float real_t;`, which CUDA and HIP input import as `var one: f32 = {};`, is the scalar's zero on every target, as if the zero were written: `float one = 0.0;` in HLSL, GLSL and Metal output and `var one: f32 = 0.0;` in WGSL output. HLSL output used to copy `{}`, which DXC rejects, WGSL output to write `array()`, which naga rejects, and GLSL output to refuse the program with `OpenGLAggregateInitializerError`; SPIR-V output refused a `half` or 16-bit one, and Metal output wrote an 8- or 16-bit one as `int(short({}))`, which the Metal compiler rejects (#3735).
+- An empty brace initializer of a variable or constant of a plain enumeration, one whose variants carry no data, such as `Mode m = {};`, which CUDA and HIP input import as `var m: Mode = {};`, is zero: `int m = 0;` in HLSL, GLSL, Metal, Slang and HIP output and `var m: i32 = 0;` in WGSL output, also for an enumeration that names its type, such as `enum Mode : uint`, whose variables these generators write as `int`. HLSL output used to copy `int m = {};`, which DXC rejects, WGSL output to write `var m: i32 = array();`, which naga rejects, and GLSL output to refuse the program with `OpenGLAggregateInitializerError`. CUDA output keeps `Mode m = {};`, which C++ value-initializes to zero (#3752).
 - WGSL output writes a declared array whose initializer gives fewer elements than the array has, such as `float a[3] = float[3](0.0);` or `{x, 1.0}`, as `array<f32, 3>(0.0, f32(), f32())`, with the elements left out set to zero as GLSL output does. It used to write `array(0.0)`, a one-element array that naga rejects.
 - WGSL output refuses an array initializer with more elements than its declared array, such as `float a[1] = {x, 1.0};` or `float a[1] = float[1](x, 1.0);`, with `WGSLAggregateInitializerError` (`project.translate.wgsl-aggregate-initializer-invalid`), which names the array type and both counts, as GLSL and HLSL output refuse it. This covers a declaration, an assignment, a return value, a call argument, a shader-scope constant, a structure member and an array of structures, and an array whose size is a constant, as in `float a[COUNT]`. It used to write `var a: array<f32, 1> = array(x, 1.0);`, which naga rejects (#3685).

diff --git a/tests/test_translator/test_enum_empty_brace_initializers.py b/tests/test_translator/test_enum_empty_brace_initializers.py
new file mode 100644
index 0000000000..0ab836d547
--- /dev/null
+++ b/tests/test_translator/test_enum_empty_brace_initializers.py
@@ -0,0 +1,113 @@
+"""An empty brace initializer of a plain enumeration is zero on the targets that write it as ``int`` (#3752).
+
+C++ value-initializes ``Mode m = {};`` to zero, and the generators write a variable of a plain enumeration as ``int``
+(``i32`` in WGSL). HLSL output copied ``int m = {};`` (DXC rejects it), WGSL output wrote ``array()`` (naga rejects
+it) and GLSL output refused it as an aggregate initializer. CUDA output declares ``Mode m`` with the enumeration type,
+for which ``{}`` is already zero, and an enumeration whose variants carry data keeps its braces.
+"""
+
+import textwrap
+
+import pytest
+
+import crosstl
+
+SHADER = textwrap.dedent("""
+    shader P {
+        enum Mode { First, Second }
+        compute {
+            buffer float* outp;
+            void main() {
+                Mode m = {};
+                outp[0] = float(int(m));
+            }
+        }
+    }
+""")
+
+KERNEL = textwrap.dedent("""
+    enum Mode { A, B };
+    extern "C" __global__ void first(float* out) {
+        Mode m = {};
+        out[0] = (float)m;
+    }
+""")
+
+EXPECTED = {
+    "directx": "int m = 0;",
+    "opengl": "int m = 0;",
+    "metal": "int m = 0;",
+    "wgsl": "var m: i32 = 0;",
+}
+
+
+def translate(tmp_path, source, backend, suffix):
+    path = tmp_path / f"shader{suffix}"
+    path.write_text(source)
+    return crosstl.translate(str(path), backend=backend, format_output=False)
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("backend", sorted(EXPECTED))
+def test_empty_brace_enum_initializer_is_zero(tmp_path, backend):
+    output = translate(tmp_path, SHADER, backend, ".cgl")
+    assert EXPECTED[backend] in output
+    assert "{}" not in output
+    assert "array()" not in output
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("backend", sorted(EXPECTED))
+def test_empty_brace_enum_initializer_from_cuda_is_zero(tmp_path, backend):
+    output = translate(tmp_path, KERNEL, backend, ".cu")
+    assert EXPECTED[backend] in output
+    assert "{}" not in output
+    assert "array()" not in output
+
+
+def test_empty_brace_enum_initializer_translates_to_spirv(tmp_path):
+    translate(tmp_path, SHADER, "spirv", ".cgl")
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("backend", sorted(EXPECTED))
+def test_empty_brace_initializer_of_an_enum_with_an_underlying_type_is_int_zero(
+    tmp_path, backend
+):
+    # The generators write a ``Mode`` variable as ``int`` whatever type the enumeration names; glslang rejects
+    # ``int m = 0u;``.
+    source = SHADER.replace("enum Mode {", "enum Mode : uint {")
+    output = translate(tmp_path, source, backend, ".cgl")
+    assert EXPECTED[backend] in output
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize(
+    "suffix, source", [(".cgl", SHADER), (".cu", KERNEL)], ids=["crossgl", "cuda"]
+)
+def test_cuda_output_keeps_the_empty_brace_initializer_of_an_enum(
+    tmp_path, suffix, source
+):
+    # CUDA output declares ``Mode m`` with the enumeration type: ``{}`` is zero there, and ``0`` does not convert.
+    output = translate(tmp_path, source, "cuda", suffix)
+    assert "Mode m = {};" in output
+
+
+PAYLOAD_ENUM = textwrap.dedent("""
+    shader P {
+        enum Mode { First(float), Second }
+        compute {
+            buffer float* outp;
+            void main() {
+                Mode m = {};
+                outp[0] = 1.0;
+            }
+        }
+    }
+""")
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("backend", ["metal", "hip", "slang"])
+def test_empty_brace_initializer_of_an_enum_with_payloads_keeps_its_braces(
+    tmp_path, backend
+):
+    # Such an enumeration is a structure on these targets, which value-initialize it from ``{}``.
+    output = translate(tmp_path, PAYLOAD_ENUM, backend, ".cgl")
+    assert "Mode m = {};" in output
+    assert "Mode m = 0;" not in output

problem_statement.title: LLM component returns an undeclared `exit_reason` output, causing a pipeline warning and an unconnectable socket
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**

The `LLM` component returns an `exit_reason` key from `run()`/`run_async()` but does not declare it in `@component.output_types`, so every pipeline run logs the framework's undeclared-output warning, the key is silently dropped, and `Pipeline.connect("llm.exit_reason", ...)` is impossible.

`haystack/components/generators/chat/llm.py:92` declares only `messages`/`last_message`/`token_usage`, while `run()` (`:164`) pops `step_count` and `tool_call_counts` but not `exit_reason`, which the `Agent` base returns from `_public_outputs` (`haystack/components/agents/agent.py:88-93, 121-123`). The `Agent` component exposes `exit_reason` as a socket; its `LLM` subclass does not.

**Error message**

```
WARNING:haystack.core.pipeline.base:Component 'llm' (type: LLM) returned output keys {'exit_reason'} that are not declared in its output types. These keys will be ignored and not passed to downstream components.

PipelineConnectError: 'llm.exit_reason' does not exist
```

Probe output:

```
keys: ['exit_reason', 'last_message', 'messages', 'token_usage']
declared outputs: ['last_message', 'messages', 'token_usage']
```

**Expected behavior**

Either expose `exit_reason` like `Agent` does (declare it in `set_output_types` so it can be connected), or remove it from the returned dict in `LLM.run`/`run_async` the same way `step_count`/`tool_call_counts` are removed — matching the `run()` docstring, which lists only the three declared outputs.

**To Reproduce**

Build a pipeline containing the `LLM` component with a scripted chat generator, run it, and inspect the missing-output warning and `Pipeline.connect("llm.exit_reason", ...)`. Repro scripts `probe_llm.py`, `probe_llm_async.py`, `probe_llm_connect.py` are available; happy to attach them.

**Additional context**

- Fix direction is a design choice (expose vs drop), hence an issue rather than a drive-by PR.
- Searched open and closed issues/PRs for `exit_reason`/undeclared outputs: nearest is #12890 (Agent `exit_reason` vs `last_message` ordering, different); closed PRs #11427/#12277 are unrelated.

**System**

- OS: Windows 11
- Haystack version: `4b5dd70` (main, v3.5.0-rc0)

Reported with AI assistance (Claude); the reproduction was executed and verified locally.

+        payload = hub.call_tool(tool_name, arguments, timeout=timeout)
+    except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
+        exc.close()
+        if exc.code == 401:
+            return False, None
+        return True, {"success": False, "error": f"hub refused {tool_name} ({exc.code})"}
+    except Exception:
+        logger.debug("hub tool call %s did not complete", tool_name, exc_info=True)
+        return True, None
+    if not isinstance(payload, dict):
+        logger.debug("hub returned no usable %s response", tool_name)
+        return True, None
+    error = payload.get("error")
+    if error:
+        message = error.get("message") if isinstance(error, dict) else None
+        return True, {"success": False, "error": message or "unknown error"}
+    try:
+        result = tool_result(payload)
+    except (KeyError, IndexError, TypeError, ValueError):
+        logger.debug("hub returned an unrecognized %s response", tool_name)
+        return True, None
+    if not isinstance(result, dict):
+        logger.debug("hub returned a non-mapping %s result", tool_name)
+        return True, None
+    return True, result

problem_statement.title: Save-hook diary checkpoint is refused while a `mempalace serve` hub holds the writer lease (3.10.0)
problem_statement.body:
**Version / platform:** mempalace 3.10.0, chromadb 1.5.9, Windows 11, Python 3.13, Claude Code harness.

**Setup:** one `mempalace serve --palace <path>` hub is the palace's only writer (as recommended for
several concurrent agent sessions). Sessions use the stdio `mempalace-mcp` proxy, which forwards to
the hub, and the Stop/PreCompact save hooks run `mempalace hook run`.

**What happens:** on every save, the transcript mine is forwarded to the hub and succeeds, but the
diary checkpoint is refused:

```
[20:46:52] TRIGGERING SAVE at exchange 15
[20:46:59] Diary checkpoint failed: another mine is in progress: palace C:\...\palace is held by PID 18872 (...\mempalace\mcp_server\__main__.py --transport http); wait for it to finish or stop the holder before retrying
mempalace: forwarding mine to palace hub http://127.0.0.1:8765 (pid 18872)
```

**Why, as far as we can tell:** `hooks_cli._save_diary_direct` calls `tool_diary_write` in-process
(around `hooks_cli.py:1110-1135`). Unlike `cmd_mine`, which hands the job to a live hub via
`_forward_mine_to_hub`, the diary path has no hub forward, so it needs the writer lease the hub
already holds. The daemon path (`write_routing`) is covered, but a hub is not.

**Impact:** transcripts are still captured (thanks to the mine forwarding added in 3.9), so the
verbatim record is intact. What is lost is the per-save diary entry, so `mempalace_diary_read` has
no checkpoints for sessions saved while a hub is running.

**Possible fix:** when `server_registry.read_live_serverinfo()` finds a live, writable hub, send the
checkpoint as a `mempalace_diary_write` tool call over HTTP, the same way `_forward_mine_to_hub`
does for mines, and keep the in-process write as the fallback when no hub is running.

Thank you for the hub forwarding and the stdio proxy in 3.8–3.9; they made a multi-session setup
workable on this machine.

+    """
+    Return the score to use in the arithmetic of a join mode.
+
+    Missing and non-finite (NaN or infinity) scores are both treated as 0. A non-finite score that reaches the
+    arithmetic of a join mode does not stay local to its own Document, it turns the scores of the other Documents
+    into NaN as well.
+    """
+    return score if score is not None and isfinite(score) else 0.0

+        # A non-finite score is read as 0, exactly like a missing score. In a list of negative
+        # scores that 0 is the highest value, so the Document with the non-finite score ends up
+        # first. This pins the "missing/0" reading so the behavior stays explicit and does not
+        # silently change when every other score is negative.
+        joiner = DocumentJoiner(join_mode="distribution_based_rank_fusion", sort_by_score=False)
+        documents = [
+            Document(content="a", score=-0.1),
+            Document(content="b", score=-0.5),
+            Document(content="non-finite", score=float("nan")),
+            Document(content="d", score=-0.9),
+        ]
+
+        output = joiner.run([documents])
+
+        assert all(math.isfinite(doc.score) for doc in output["documents"])
+        scores_by_content = {doc.content: doc.score for doc in output["documents"]}
+        assert (
+            scores_by_content["non-finite"] > scores_by_content["a"] > scores_by_content["b"] > scores_by_content["d"]
+        )
+
+    def test_distribution_based_rank_fusion_handles_a_list_of_non_finite_scores(self):
+        joiner = DocumentJoiner(join_mode="distribution_based_rank_fusion", sort_by_score=False)
+
+        output = joiner.run([[Document(content="a", score=float("nan")), Document(content="b", score=float("inf"))]])
+
+        assert [doc.score for doc in output["documents"]] == [0.0, 0.0]
+
+    def test_distribution_based_rank_fusion_warns_about_non_finite_scores(self, caplog):
+        joiner = DocumentJoiner(join_mode="distribution_based_rank_fusion")
+        documents = [Document(content="a", score=0.9), Document(content="b", score=float("nan"))]
+
+        with caplog.at_level(logging.WARNING):
+            joiner.run([documents])
+
+        assert "have a non-finite score" in caplog.text
+        assert documents[1].id in caplog.text
+        assert documents[0].id not in caplog.text
+

problem_statement.title: [Bug]: DocumentJoiner in distribution_based_rank_fusion mode turns every score of a list into NaN when one score is not finite
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**

`DocumentJoiner` with `join_mode="distribution_based_rank_fusion"` rescales the scores of each input list with the mean and the standard deviation of that list. Both statistics are computed from the raw scores, so a single score that is `NaN` or infinite makes `mean_score`, `std_dev` and `delta_score` non-finite, and the rescaled score of *every* Document in that list becomes `NaN`.

Nothing is logged and nothing is raised, so the run looks successful: a list of four ordered scores goes in, four `NaN` scores come out.

```python
from haystack import Document
from haystack.components.joiners import DocumentJoiner

docs = [
    Document(content="a", score=0.9),
    Document(content="b", score=0.5),
    Document(content="c", score=float("nan")),   # e.g. from a custom retriever
    Document(content="d", score=0.2),
]
out = DocumentJoiner(join_mode="distribution_based_rank_fusion").run([docs])["documents"]
print("joined :", [(d.content, d.score) for d in out])
print("kept   :", [d.content for d in out if d.score >= 0.5])
```

Actual output:

```text
joined : [('a', nan), ('b', nan), ('c', nan), ('d', nan)]
kept   : []
```

**Error message**

None. The failure is silent and only shows up in whatever consumes the scores next. `inf` and `-inf` reproduce it as well.

**Expected behavior**

A score that carries no ranking information is already handled by this mode: `score=None` is treated as `0`, and there is a test pinning that behavior (`test_run_with_distribution_based_rank_fusion_join_mode_with_none_score`). A non-finite score is the same kind of unusable value, so it should be treated the same way and leave the other Documents with meaningful rescaled scores:

```text
joined : [('a', 0.7457...), ('b', 0.5491...), ('d', 0.4017...), ('c', 0.3034...)]
kept   : ['a', 'b']
```

**Additional context**

- Neither `Document` nor `Document.from_dict` validates `score`, and `json.loads` accepts the `NaN`/`Infinity` literals, so a Document that came through a dump written by another tool can already carry a non-finite score.
- A custom retriever or reranker that emits a non-finite score is the more likely source. `InMemoryEmbeddingRetriever` is not one: a zero vector scores `0.0` there.
- This is the same class of defect as #13410 (non-finite `DocumentJoiner` *weights*) and #13508 (non-finite `MetaFieldRanker` weight), both fixed by rejecting the invalid value at construction time. Scores have no constructor to validate against, and raising in `run()` would break pipelines that may currently "run", so treating the value like the missing score this mode already handles looks like the smaller change.

**To Reproduce**

Run the snippet above; swap `float("nan")` for `float("inf")` or `float("-inf")` for the other two cases.

**FAQ Check**
- [ ] Have you had a look at [our new FAQ page](https://docs.haystack.deepset.ai/docs/faq)?

**System:**
- OS: Windows 11
- Haystack version: 3.4.1 (same expression as `main` at `d9e7e70`)

problem_statement.title: Anthropic /v1/messages rejects redacted_thinking blocks in assistant history with a 400
problem_statement.body:
**Impact:** Anthropic-compatible clients that replay a `redacted_thinking` block from an earlier turn (Anthropic SDK apps, or a Claude Code session resumed after using a cloud model) get HTTP 400 and the turn stops. `redacted_thinking` is part of the documented Messages API history contract: clients must send it back unchanged.

**Severity:** P1 — **Frequency:** any request whose assistant history contains a `redacted_thinking` block (4 of 4 runs, non-stream and stream, with and without `thinking` enabled).

**Version:** rapid-mlx 1.0.2, `pip install rapid-mlx==1.0.2`, macOS 26.5.1, Apple M4 Pro 48 GB, model qwen3.5-4b-4bit.

**Repro:**
1. `rapid-mlx serve qwen3.5-4b-4bit --port 8000`
2. Send this Messages request (a normal two-turn tool loop whose assistant turn also contains a redacted thinking block):

```bash
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/messages \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"default","max_tokens":300,"tools":[{"name":"shell","description":"Run a shell command","input_schema":{"type":"object","properties":{"command":{"type":"string"}},"required":["command"]}}],"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Use the shell tool to run pwd."},{"role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"redacted_thinking","data":"ENCRYPTEDDATA"},{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_1","name":"shell","input":{"command":"pwd"}}]},{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"tool_result","tool_use_id":"toolu_1","content":"/tmp\n"}]}]}'
```

**Expected / Actual:** Expected HTTP 200 and a normal assistant reply (the opaque block accepted and preserved or ignored, the same way a `thinking` block is accepted). Actual HTTP 400 and the Anthropic SDK raises `BadRequestError`.

**Evidence:**
```
HTTP 400
{"type":"error","error":{"message":"Invalid request body: messages.1.content: Input should be a valid string; messages.1.content.0: Value error, content[].type 'redacted_thinking' is not a recognized Anthropic content block type. Allowed types: ['document', 'image', 'text', 'thinking', 'tool_result', 'tool_use']."}}
```
The identical request with the `redacted_thinking` block removed returns 200; with `{"type":"thinking","thinking":"...","signature":"..."}` instead it also returns 200.

**Likely cause:** `rapid_mlx/api/anthropic_models.py:43` — `_ANTHROPIC_CONTENT_BLOCK_TYPES` omits `redacted_thinking`. Add it (required field `data`) and treat the opaque payload as pass-through/ignored in the adapter.

problem_statement.title: [BUG] LinearRegression get_estimator method's required arguments appear to do nothing
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**

No matter what is passed into the [get_estimator](https://unit8co.github.io/darts/_modules/darts/models/forecasting/regression_model.html#RegressionModel.get_estimator) method of the LinearRegression class the same model object is returned.

**To Reproduce**

```python
from darts import TimeSeries
from darts.models.forecasting.linear_regression_model import RegressionModel
from darts.utils.timeseries_generation import linear_timeseries

import numpy as np

trend = linear_timeseries(start_value=0, end_value=100, length=100)
noise = TimeSeries.from_times_and_values(
    trend.time_index, np.random.normal(0, 5, size=trend.values().shape)
)

series = trend + noise

model = RegressionModel(lags=3, output_chunk_length=2)
model.fit(series)

print(id(model.get_estimator(1, 1)))
print(id(model.get_estimator(2, 2)))
print(id(model.get_estimator(-1e7, -1e7)))
print(id(model.get_estimator(1e7, 1e7)))
```
```
13699865568
13699865568
13699865568
13699865568
```

**Expected behavior**
My assumption was that a Darts model would build 1 underlying model per future time period, i.e. "direct forecasting". `get_regressor` takes 2 arguments:

```python
    def get_estimator(self, horizon: int, target_dim: int):
        """Returns the estimator that forecasts the `horizon`th step of the `target_dim`th target component.

        The model is returned directly if it supports multi-output natively.

        Parameters
        ----------
        horizon
            The index of the forecasting point within `output_chunk_length`.
        target_dim
            The index of the target component.
        """
```

No matter the arguments passed in the method will...
1) return an object without an error, even if the inputs are ridiculous
2) return the same model object (not sure which horizon's model this is).

Both are unexpected to me.

**System (please complete the following information):**
 - Python version: 3.12
 - darts version: 0.30.0

**Additional context**
New to darts.

problem_statement.title: AugMix ignores its seed argument when choosing augmentations
problem_statement.body:
`AugMix` accepts a `seed` argument, documents it as "Used to create a random seed" and serializes it in `get_config`, but the seed does not reach the line that picks which augmentations to apply. Two layers built with the same seed produce different outputs.

```python
import numpy as np
import keras
from keras import layers

x = np.random.randint(0, 256, (2, 8, 8, 3)).astype("float32")
a = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(layers.AugMix(seed=1234)(x))
b = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(layers.AugMix(seed=1234)(x))
np.abs(a - b).max()
# non-zero
```

Inside `get_random_transformation`, line 226 resolves the layer seed and lines 228-236 pass it to the Dirichlet and Beta draws, while lines 250-255 pass a seed down to each sub-layer. Line 242 is the only draw that receives nothing: `layer_name = py_random.choice(self._augment_layers + [None])` reaches for the `random` module instead.

`AugMix` is the only layer under `keras/src/layers/` that imports Python's `random` module at all. `RandAugment` makes the same kind of choice from the same kind of list one file over, seeded, through `self.backend.random.randint(..., seed=self._get_seed_generator(...))` at lines 179-184, and both layers carry the identical docstring line for `seed`.

`aug_mix_test.py` has four tests. `test_random_augment_randomness` checks only that the output differs from the input and passes no seed, and the `"seed": 43` in `test_layer` is a `run_layer_test` kwarg, so nothing ever asserted that the same seed gives the same output.

`keras.utils.set_random_seed` does seed the global `random`, so a program that sets it globally is unaffected. It is the layer's own `seed` argument that has no effect here.

Happy to send the PR

problem_statement.title: Save configured sdists with a standard filename
problem_statement.body:
Some supported `source:` configurations fail to download source, or save it under a name that later commands cannot find. This prevents the package from building.

Examples:
- A `hook-sdist` resolver hook returns a tag archive URL ending in `/v1.0`. With no download hook, the download fails with `InvalidSdistFilename`.
- `pypi-download` with `download_kind: sdist` saves `pkg-v1.0.tar.gz`. Later, `find_sdist()` searches for `pkg-1.0.tar.gz` and finds nothing.

**Expected:** Save the archive using the package name and resolved version, preserving `.tar.gz` or `.zip`. Both cases should work without a custom download hook. Add regression tests for both cases.

Observed on `new-resolver-config` at `ff8d7683`. Related: #1414 — [review comment](https://github.com/python-wheel-build/fromager/pull/1414#discussion_r4443496023).

problem_statement.title: [BUG] MJCF importer ignores compiler mass and inertia guards
problem_statement.body:
## Description

`ModelBuilder.add_mjcf()` currently ignores the MJCF compiler attributes `boundmass`, `boundinertia`, and `balanceinertia`. As a result, imported body mass properties can differ from a native MuJoCo compilation.

## Expected behavior

Apply the compiler lower bounds after body mass properties have been accumulated, and either balance or reject principal inertias that violate the triangle inequality according to `balanceinertia`. The settings should affect only bodies created by the current MJCF import.

## Reproduction

Import a body with `mass="0.1"` under `<compiler boundmass="0.5"/>`, or a body with `diaginertia="0.01 0.01 0.1"` under `<compiler balanceinertia="true"/>`. Newton keeps the authored values, while MuJoCo compiles them to `0.5` and `0.04 0.04 0.04`, respectively.

## Proposed fix

Parse the three compiler attributes, post-process only the imported body range using MuJoCo's ordering, update inverse mass/inertia, and add native-MuJoCo comparison tests.

Grouping now keeps each carried scalar's multiplicity on pandas and Polars instead of returning null groups or dropping a connected result group (#2252).

+    assert edge_pairs(seeded_two_hop) == expected
+    for out in (unseeded, seeded_two_hop):
+        assert str(out._edges["s"].dtype) == "Int64"
+        assert str(out._edges["d"].dtype) == "Int64"
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("node_null", [False, True])
+@pytest.mark.parametrize(
+    "direction,seed",
+    [("reverse", 2**53 + 1), ("undirected", 2**53)],
+)
+def test_direct_hop_directions_keep_native_edge_ids_with_nullable_nodes(
+    direction, seed, node_null
+):
+    base = 2**53
+    neighbor = base + 1
+    node_ids = [None, base, neighbor] if node_null else [base, neighbor]
+    nodes = pd.DataFrame({"id": pd.array(node_ids, dtype="Int64")})
+    edges = pd.DataFrame(
+        {
+            "s": pd.Series([base], dtype="int64"),
+            "d": pd.Series([neighbor], dtype="int64"),
+        }
+    )
+    graph = graphistry.nodes(nodes, "id").edges(edges, "s", "d")
+    seed_nodes = pd.DataFrame({"id": pd.array([seed], dtype="Int64")})
+
+    out = graph.hop(
+        nodes=seed_nodes,
+        hops=1,
+        direction=direction,
+        engine="pandas",
+    )
+
+    assert set(zip(out._edges["s"].tolist(), out._edges["d"].tolist())) == {
+        (base, neighbor)
+    }
+    assert str(out._edges["s"].dtype) == "int64"
+    assert str(out._edges["d"].dtype) == "int64"

problem_statement.title: GFQL fallback drops nullable 64-bit ID matches with pandas 3.1 / NumPy 2.5
problem_statement.body:
## Bug

The GFQL fallback path silently drops valid rows when the graph uses nullable 64-bit integer node identifiers with the current pandas/NumPy release pair. The indexed/fast path returns the expected row. This blocks [tck-gfql #212](https://github.com/graphistry/tck-gfql/pull/212)'s hosted CI before its new scenarios execute, but reproduces on unchanged TCK main; #212 did not introduce it.

## Source-proven reproduction

- Product: pygraphistry master `a649e05f20a2457a024722b78b6f99d3ab0aeb46`.
- TCK: main `e5bd3a2a45729c8957fc1fa71ddd22121bbc82e1`, existing `tests/cypher_tck/test_nullable_identifier_identity.py`.
- Hosted-like local env: Python 3.12.10, NumPy 2.5.4, pandas 3.1.0, pytest 9.1.1, editable exact product source. Hosted [CI run 40902482631](https://github.com/graphistry/tck-gfql/actions/runs/40902482631) used Python 3.12.15 with the same package versions and failed the same case.
- Command from TCK main: `/tmp/tck-2253-hosted-uv-env/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/cypher_tck/test_nullable_identifier_identity.py -k pandas --tb=no`. The test builds nullable `Int64`/`UInt64` node and edge IDs (including nulls), creates node/edge indexes, then queries `n(id=big+offset) -> e_forward() -> n() -> rows(source="b")` with all registered routes on or off.

| Environment | Routes on | Routes off, valid seeds 0/1 | Routes off, empty seed 2 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| NumPy 2.2.6 / pandas 2.3.3 | 6/6 pass | 4/4 pass | 2/2 pass |
| NumPy 2.5.4 / pandas 3.1.0 | 6/6 pass | **4/4 fail** | 2/2 pass |

For both `Int64` near 2^53 and `UInt64` near 2^63, the failing fallback cases expect one matched destination but return zero rows. Running just the first failing test against both TCK main and #212 produces the same result. The package-pair boundary is proven; pandas versus NumPy as the individual cause is not yet isolated.

## Acceptance

- Find and fix the generalized nullable/exact-integer ID loss in the fallback path; preserve identity and row counts across route-on/off, null placements, Int64/UInt64, and values beyond float exactness. Avoid a special case keyed to this test.
- Add positive valid-seed, partial/null, and empty negative oracles on both sides of the changed boundary. Validate pandas under both package pairs; check Polars, Polars-GPU, and cuDF where the changed code path applies, or record a precise nonapplicability/typed decline.
- Preserve static typing and existing index semantics. If a hot path or index route changes, add a source-pinned pyg-bench parity/performance control before claiming no regression.
- Require focused tests, exact-head hosted CI/TCK, and DGX GPU validation where applicable before landing. Coordinate with #2253/#212; do not mask the failure by pinning TCK CI to older pandas without a separate support-floor decision.

Related but distinct: #1890 tracks other pandas-3 latents and CI gaps; closed #2058 tracked route-dependent integer dtype upcasting.

problem_statement.title: CPLEX: Optimal solution with unscaled infeasibilities is thrown out
problem_statement.body:
Hi everyone, I have an issue with CPLEX. for some problems, which Highs can solve, I get an unknown status from linopy, with the message that the problem is optimal with unscaled infeasibilities. As I understand, CPLEX introduced the solution of the scaled problem to the unscaled problem, and there were some slight infeasibilities, which usually do not mean a lot (see for examle here: http://iea-etsap.org/forum/showthread.php?tid=162)

Linopy, however, seems to not import this solution, potentially because the status is unknown and not optimal. Would it be possible to change this, so that linopy simply imports this solution, even though there might be slight infeasibilities?

Best,
Georg

problem_statement.title: Implement a search by comment function
problem_statement.body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Many times MCNP objects are identifiable by their comments, and less so their number. It's desirable to be able to find objects by what their comments contain. 



## Describe the solution you'd like

I was thinking in `NumberedObjectCollection` (also it may be time to make `MCNP_Problem.data_inputs` its own class) of implementing something like:

``` python
import re

def get_by_comment(self, searcher: str | re.Pattern): -> Generator[MCNP_Object, None, None]
     pass
```

Or also possible following `montepy.Materials.get_containing_(all|any)` where you can search by multiple strings. 

## Describe alternatives you've considered

For now users can just do this manually (after #972).

## Additional context

This is a follow-on to #185.

+def _furniture_statements(doc: DoclingDocument) -> list[list[tuple[str, str | None]]]:
+    """Return the (text, hyperlink) runs of each furniture text, in document order.
+
+    The runs of a text with styling or links share an inline group.
+    """
+    statements: dict[str, list[tuple[str, str | None]]] = {}
+    for item in doc.texts:
+        if item.content_layer != ContentLayer.FURNITURE:
+            continue
+        key = item.self_ref
+        if item.parent is not None:
+            parent = item.parent.resolve(doc)
+            if parent.label == GroupLabel.INLINE:
+                assert parent.content_layer == ContentLayer.FURNITURE
+                key = parent.self_ref
+        statements.setdefault(key, []).append(
+            (item.text, str(item.hyperlink) if item.hyperlink is not None else None)
+        )
+    return list(statements.values())
+
+
+def test_jats_license_and_funding_statements_are_furniture():
+    doc = convert_jats_article_meta(
+        """
+      <title-group><article-title>Control</article-title></title-group>
+      <permissions><license xlink:href="https://example.org/c3-licence"><license-p>CHARLIE-LICENCE terms of the
+      <ext-link ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://example.org/c3-licence">licence</ext-link>.</license-p></license></permissions>
+      <abstract><p>CHARLIE-ABSTRACT paragraph.</p></abstract>
+      <funding-group><funding-statement>CHARLIE-FUNDING statement.</funding-statement></funding-group>
+""",
+        "<sec><title>S</title><p>Body.</p></sec>",
+    )
+
+    assert _furniture_statements(doc) == [
+        [
+            ("CHARLIE-LICENCE terms of the ", None),
+            ("licence", "https://example.org/c3-licence"),
+            (".", None),
+        ],
+        [("CHARLIE-FUNDING statement.", None)],
+    ]
+    # The default export keeps to the body.
+    body_markdown = doc.export_to_markdown()
+    assert "CHARLIE-ABSTRACT paragraph." in body_markdown
+    assert "CHARLIE-LICENCE" not in body_markdown
+    assert "CHARLIE-FUNDING" not in body_markdown
+    # On request, the statements follow the article content.
+    markdown = doc.export_to_markdown(
+        included_content_layers={ContentLayer.BODY, ContentLayer.FURNITURE}
+    )
+    assert (
+        markdown.index("Body.")
+        < markdown.index("CHARLIE-LICENCE")
+        < markdown.index("CHARLIE-FUNDING")
+    )
+
+
+def test_jats_copyright_and_each_license_paragraph_are_kept_in_order():
+    doc = convert_jats_article_meta(
+        """
+      <title-group><article-title>Permissions</article-title></title-group>
+      <permissions>
+        <copyright-statement>© The Authors 2026.</copyright-statement>
+        <copyright-year>2026</copyright-year>
+        <license license-type="cc-by" xlink:href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">
+          <license-p>Distributed under the CC BY licence.</license-p>
+          <license-p>Funded by SCOAP<sup>3</sup></license-p>
+        </license>
+      </permissions>
+      <funding-group>
+        <award-group><funding-source>Agency</funding-source></award-group>
+        <funding-statement>First grant.</funding-statement>
+        <funding-statement>Second grant.</funding-statement>
+      </funding-group>
+"""
+    )

+    assert _furniture_statements(doc) == [
+        [("© The Authors 2026.", None)],
+        [("Distributed under the CC BY licence.", None)],
+        [("Funded by SCOAP", None), ("3", None)],
+        [("First grant.", None)],
+        [("Second grant.", None)],
+    ]
+    superscripts = [
+        item.text
+        for item in doc.texts
+        if item.formatting is not None and item.formatting.script == Script.SUPER
+    ]
+    assert superscripts == ["3"]

problem_statement.title: JATS: licence and funding statements in `<article-meta>` are not converted
problem_statement.body:
### Bug A follow-up to #3583. From ``, the backend reads the title, authors and abstract (`_parse_metadata`, [`jats_backend.py#L527-L534` at v2.138.0](https://github.com/docling-project/docling/blob/a76ae4b6acfbb7e9a63b9f8592f05d555e8c3a27/docling/backend/xml/jats_backend.py#L527-L534)). Other article-level statements are not represented, including: - `permissions/license/license-p`, and its links; - `funding-group/funding-statement`. These are visible in the published article. Downstream users often need them, for example the licence that governs reuse of the text. Minimal input (after the prologue): ```xml Control CHARLIE-LICENCE terms of the licence.

CHARLIE-ABSTRACT paragraph.

 CHARLIE-FUNDING statement. S

Body.

 ``` **Observed** on v2.138.0 (`a76ae4b6`) and on `main` (`f0d90989`), unchanged since 2.131.0: - the abstract is converted; - `CHARLIE-LICENCE`, `CHARLIE-FUNDING` and the licence URL appear nowhere in `export_to_dict()`. Is this intended scope for the JATS backend? If these statements belong in the document, where would you want them: body text, a furniture or metadata layer, or something else? problem_statement.title: Tokenizers with a TRL training chat template are rejected for tool calling: Unrecognized chat template
problem_statement.body:
`add_response_schema` recognizes a model by comparing its chat template, character for character, with a copy stored in `trl/chat_templates/`. It only matches the original templates, not the training variants TRL ships alongside them (the ones `get_training_chat_template` returns). A tokenizer that carries a training template is therefore rejected, and `GRPOTrainer` with tools fails at init. This happens for a tokenizer saved after SFT with the training template set as its chat template, e.g. via `SFTConfig(chat_template_path=...)` or by assigning `tokenizer.chat_template`.

### Reproduction

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from trl import add_response_schema, get_training_chat_template

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct")
tokenizer.chat_template = get_training_chat_template(tokenizer)
add_response_schema(tokenizer)
```

```
ValueError: Unrecognized chat template, failed to add response schema. Please manually set the response schema on the tokenizer or processor. See the Transformers [docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/chat_response_parsing#response-parsing) for more details on response parsing.
```

The same call succeeds with the original chat template. Tested with TRL `main` and transformers 5.20.2.

### Affected training templates

Every training template whose original template `add_response_schema` recognizes: `deepseek_r1_distill`, `glm4moe`, `gptoss`, `lfm2_v2`, `nemotron_3_nano`, `nemotron_3_super`, `nemotron_3_ultra`, `nemotron_3_5_lightning`, `qwen2_5`, `qwen3`, `qwen3_instruct_2507`, `qwen3_vl`, `qwen3_5_nothink`, `qwen3_5_think`, `qwen3_6` and `qwen3_8`.

Same matching as #7943 and #7492, but here the template is one TRL itself provides.

problem_statement.title: BUG: Possible coefficient scaling mismatch in HSGPPeriodic prior (q_j^2 used as std)
problem_statement.body:
## Bug summary
`HSGPPeriodic` appears to apply periodic basis coefficients at the wrong scale, which can distort the GP prior variance and produce systematically incorrect prior draws.

This is not a cosmetic mismatch: it can change model behavior and inference quality whenever users rely on `HSGPPeriodic` as an approximation to `gp.Latent` with a periodic kernel.

## Why this is high impact
- It affects **prior correctness** for a core GP approximation API.
- It can bias uncertainty and function amplitudes before seeing any data.
- It directly undermines the expected equivalence between `HSGPPeriodic` and full periodic GP priors.

## Evidence in code
### 1) Coefficients are documented/returned as variance-level terms (`q_j^2`)
- `pymc/gp/cov.py` (`Periodic.power_spectral_density_approx`): docs and implementation indicate coefficients correspond to \(\tilde q_j^2\).

### 2) Same coefficients are used as if they were std-level terms
- `pymc/gp/hsgp_approx.py` (`HSGPPeriodic.prior_linearized`, `prior`, `_build_conditional`): coefficients are multiplied directly into `beta ~ Normal(0,1)` via terms like `phi @ (coeff * beta)`.

If `coeff = q_j^2`, then variance contribution becomes `(q_j^2)^2` instead of `q_j^2`.

## Observable symptom
The periodic prior equivalence test is currently xfailed:
- `tests/gp/test_hsgp_approx.py::TestHSGPPeriodic::test_prior`

A scaling mismatch is a plausible root cause of this persistent mismatch.

## Expected behavior
When `beta ~ Normal(0,1)`, basis multipliers should be **std-level** coefficients.
If the covariance helper returns variance-level coefficients (`q_j^2`), `HSGPPeriodic` should use `sqrt(q_j^2)` at the multiplication site.

## Suggested fix direction
- Option A (minimal): keep `power_spectral_density_approx` as variance-level output and apply `pt.sqrt(...)` in `HSGPPeriodic` where coefficients multiply `beta`.
- Option B: change semantics/API so the helper returns std-level coefficients consistently, then update naming/docs accordingly.

Either way, resolving this should help un-xfail periodic prior equivalence and restore expected approximation behavior.

problem_statement.title: Codex 0.166 hooks silently record zero exchanges
problem_statement.body:
MemPalace 3.11.0 automatic capture is incompatible with current Codex CLI 0.166.0 rollouts.

Reproduction:
1. Install the documented Codex SessionStart, Stop, and PreCompact hooks.
2. Start a Codex session and exchange several user and assistant messages.
3. Let Stop or PreCompact run.

Observed hook log:

    Session ...: 0 exchanges, 0 since last save

The hook is installed and firing. Current Codex rollouts store conversation messages as top-level response_item records whose payload is type=message with role=user or role=assistant and input_text/output_text content blocks. MemPalace 3.11.0 normalize._try_codex_jsonl and hooks_cli._count_human_messages only recognise the older event_msg user_message/agent_message representation. Consequently the advertised background auto-save silently saves nothing.

A one-time compatibility converter confirmed the diagnosis: converting response_item message records into the old event_msg representation allowed the same sessions to mine successfully (20 sessions, 1,234 drawers). The converter excluded reasoning, tool calls, tool outputs, developer instructions, and non-user synthetic context.

Expected: current Codex rollouts are recognised automatically, actual user-authored messages are distinguished from synthetic role=user context using content_item_kinds/provenance, and failures are surfaced instead of reported as a normal zero-exchange save.

problem_statement.title: [Bug]: resolve_coupled_variables=True breaks for boundary conditions and modifies the input model
problem_statement.body:
### PyBaMM Version

main

### Python Version

3.14

### Describe the bug

There are two bugs, which both happen when `pybamm.Discretisation(resolve_coupled_variables=True)` is used. This is not the default, so none of the existing functionality is affected.


### 1. A `CoupledVariable` in a boundary condition is never resolved

`process_model` discretises boundary conditions (`process_boundary_conditions`) before it calls `_resolve_coupled_variables_in_model`. The boundary conditions therefore still contain the `CoupledVariable` when they are discretised.

### 2. `inplace=False` still rewrites the input model's equations

The resolve step writes the resolved expressions into the `model` that was passed in, not into the copy that gets discretised. The user's model is changed even with `inplace=False`. Assigning into the copy would not be enough either, because `BaseModel.new_copy` only copies `boundary_conditions` one level deep and the per-boundary dicts are shared.

```python
model = pybamm.BaseModel()
a, b = pybamm.Variable("a"), pybamm.Variable("b")
rhs_a = -pybamm.CoupledVariable("b")
model.rhs = {a: rhs_a, b: pybamm.Scalar(1)}
model.initial_conditions = {a: pybamm.Scalar(1), b: pybamm.Scalar(0)}
model.variables = {"a": a, "b": b}

pybamm.Discretisation(resolve_coupled_variables=True).process_model(model, inplace=False)
assert model.rhs[a] is rhs_a  # fails
```

### Steps to Reproduce

### 1. A `CoupledVariable` in a boundary condition is never resolved

```python
import pybamm

model = pybamm.BaseModel()
c = pybamm.Variable("c", domain="negative electrode")
model.rhs = {c: pybamm.div(pybamm.grad(c))}
model.boundary_conditions = {
    c: {
        "left": (pybamm.Scalar(0), "Neumann"),
        "right": (pybamm.CoupledVariable("Flux"), "Neumann"),
    }
}
model.initial_conditions = {c: pybamm.Scalar(1)}
model.variables = {"Flux": pybamm.Scalar(2), "c": c}

geometry = pybamm.Geometry(
    {"negative electrode": {"x_n": {"min": pybamm.Scalar(0), "max": pybamm.Scalar(1)}}}
)
mesh = pybamm.Mesh(geometry, {"negative electrode": pybamm.Uniform1DSubMesh}, {"x_n": 10})
disc = pybamm.Discretisation(
    mesh, {"negative electrode": pybamm.FiniteVolume()}, resolve_coupled_variables=True
)
disc.process_model(model)
```

```
pybamm.expression_tree.exceptions.DiscretisationError: CoupledVariable 'Flux' was not
resolved before discretisation. Ensure the variable exists in model.variables.
```

### 2. `inplace=False` still rewrites the input model's equations


```python
model = pybamm.BaseModel()
a, b = pybamm.Variable("a"), pybamm.Variable("b")
rhs_a = -pybamm.CoupledVariable("b")
model.rhs = {a: rhs_a, b: pybamm.Scalar(1)}
model.initial_conditions = {a: pybamm.Scalar(1), b: pybamm.Scalar(0)}
model.variables = {"a": a, "b": b}

pybamm.Discretisation(resolve_coupled_variables=True).process_model(model, inplace=False)
assert model.rhs[a] is rhs_a  # fails
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
See above
```


### Fix

I have a fix ready to open as a PR, I will open it in case it facilitates the discussion:

- Resolve before the boundary conditions are discretised.
- With `inplace=False`, resolve into a copy of the model.
- Build new equation dicts instead of writing into the existing ones.

The PR includes regression tests for both bugs.

## Proposal: make `resolve_coupled_variables=True` the default

Because the default is `False`, a model that uses a `CoupledVariable` in its equations fails to discretise unless the user passes `discretisation_kwargs={"resolve_coupled_variables": True}` every time. `CoupledVariable`s in `model.variables` already work without it. I was told the default is `False` because of a concern of higher computational costs.

I tried timing both options. When a model has no `CoupledVariable`s, the resolve pass returns the identical expression objects. The discretised model is the same, so solve time is unaffected and the only cost is one tree walk at build time. None of the built-in models use `CoupledVariable`, so for them this cost is pure overhead.

All times are medians over 5 runs.

- **Resolve** is the resolve pass timed on its own on the parameterised model, i.e. the extra work the flag adds.
- **Disc off / on** is `Discretisation.process_model` with the flag off and on. The runs were interleaved.
- **Build + solve** is `Simulation.solve([0, 3600])` with the default solver, timed once per model.

| Model | Equations | Unique nodes | Resolve | Disc off | Disc on | Resolve / disc | Build + solve | Resolve / build + solve |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SPM | 20 | 23 | 0.2 ms | 0.119 s | 0.123 s | 0.15% | 0.12 s | 0.14% |
| SPMe | 24 | 100 | 0.6 ms | 0.181 s | 0.207 s | 0.32% | 0.16 s | 0.37% |
| DFN | 30 | 335 | 2.3 ms | 0.194 s | 0.200 s | 1.17% | 0.22 s | 1.04% |
| DFN + lumped thermal | 32 | 392 | 3.0 ms | 0.244 s | 0.227 s | 1.23% | 0.48 s | 0.63% |
| DFN + x-full thermal ¹ | 38 | 658 | 5.0 ms | 0.304 s | 0.306 s | 1.64% | 0.41 s | 1.22% |
| DFN composite anode ² | 42 | 439 | 2.5 ms | 0.266 s | 0.269 s | 0.95% | 0.42 s | 0.60% |
| SPMe + degradation ³ | 42 | 395 | 2.4 ms | 0.266 s | 0.266 s | 0.92% | 0.66 s | 0.37% |
| DFN + degradation ³ | 52 | 419 | 4.5 ms | 0.304 s | 0.300 s | 1.49% | 0.68 s | 0.67% |
| DFN + degradation + lumped thermal ³ | 54 | 493 | 4.7 ms | 0.323 s | 0.331 s | 1.47% | 2.55 s | 0.19% |
| DFN 1+1D pouch + x-lumped thermal ¹ | 42 | 685 | 5.0 ms | 0.620 s | 0.634 s | 0.80% | 2.74 s | 0.18% |

¹ Marquis2019. ² Chen2020_composite, `"particle phases": ("2", "1")`. ³ OKane2022 with SEI (solvent-diffusion limited), SEI porosity change, partially reversible lithium plating, plating porosity change, swelling and cracking, SEI on cracks, and stress-driven loss of active material. All other models use Chen2020.

The resolve pass takes 0.2–5 ms, which is at most 1.6% of discretisation and at most 1.2% of build + solve. It is smaller than the run-to-run noise: the gap between the off and on discretisation timings ranges from −7% to +14%.

**Changes needed to flip the default:**
- Change the default in `Discretisation.__init__`.
- Update `test_unresolved_coupled_variable_in_rhs_raises_error`. With the flag on, a missing coupled variable fails earlier, with `ValueError: CoupledVariable '...' not found in model.variables` instead of the `DiscretisationError`.
- Simplify `examples/scripts/coupled_variable_example.py` and the docs where they tell users to pass the flag.

### Making the resolve pass cheaper: share one cache across equations

`_resolve_coupled_variables_in_model` calls `BaseModel._resolve_coupled_variables` once per equation, and each call starts a fresh `tree_map` cache. Subtrees shared between equations, such as concentrations and potentials, are walked once per equation that uses them, so the pass visits 3–4× as many nodes as are unique (e.g. 2,285 visits for 685 unique nodes in the pouch model). It also re-resolves a coupled variable's target tree, which can be large (e.g. `"Voltage [V]"`), once per equation that references it.

Passing one cache dict through every `tree_map` call in the pass, including the recursive call that resolves a coupled variable's target, makes it 2.5–3.4× faster. Each timing is the median of 30 alternating runs of the resolve pass on its own:

| Model | Per-equation cache (current) | Shared cache | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| DFN | 2.13 ms | 0.86 ms | 2.47× |
| DFN + x-full thermal ¹ | 4.83 ms | 1.66 ms | 2.91× |
| DFN + degradation + lumped thermal ³ | 4.64 ms | 1.36 ms | 3.41× |
| DFN 1+1D pouch + x-lumped thermal ¹ | 5.05 ms | 1.81 ms | 2.78× |

The resolved equations are equal in both modes. The cache is keyed by symbol equality, so it may return an equal node from another equation instead of the original object; PyBaMM already treats equal symbols as interchangeable. With no coupled variables, this saves only 1–3 ms per build. The larger gain should come in models that do use coupled variables, because each target is resolved once instead of once per equation; that case is not measured here.

Environment: WSL2 on Linux 6.18, 8 cores, 7 GB RAM, Python 3.14, current `main` (8c6816d27). The benchmark script is available on request.

title: fix: keep channel_props functions from being shadowed by their submodules
issue_title: Functions in channel_props can be shadowed by their submodules ("'module' object is not callable")

install_config.install: pip install -e . -q && pip install pytest pytest-cov -q

gold_patch:
diff --git a/toqito/channel_props/__init__.py b/toqito/channel_props/__init__.py
index 0674af1631..cdf58eb5f4 100644
--- a/toqito/channel_props/__init__.py
+++ b/toqito/channel_props/__init__.py
@@ -2,6 +2,7 @@
 
 from importlib import import_module
 import sys
+import types
 
 __all__ = [
     "channel_dim",
@@ -30,3 +31,21 @@ def __getattr__(name: str) -> object:
 
 def __dir__() -> list[str]:
     return sorted(__all__)
+
+
+class _ChannelPropsModule(types.ModuleType):
+    """Keep the public functions from being replaced by their submodules.
+
+    Each function lives in a submodule of the same name. Importing such a submodule directly (as other
+    `toqito` modules do, e.g. `from toqito.channel_props.channel_dim import channel_dim`) makes Python
+    set the submodule as an attribute of this package. That attribute would then hide the function, so
+    `from toqito.channel_props import channel_dim` would return the module instead of the function.
+    """
+
+    def __setattr__(self, name: str, value: object) -> None:
+        if name in __all__ and isinstance(value, types.ModuleType):
+            value = getattr(value, name, value)
+        super().__setattr__(name, value)
+
+
+sys.modules[__name__].__class__ = _ChannelPropsModule

+

+from toqito import channel_props
+
